title: St Louis-Style Pork Ribs
subtitle: Dry-rubbed spare ribs cooked low and slow in the oven
excerpt: St Louis-style ribs are spare ribs trimmed into a neat, flat rack with the tips and sternum bone removed. They cook long and low in the oven until the meat pulls back from the bone and the dry rub sets into a dark, spiced crust. Saucing them at the end is optional.
sourceNotes: St Louis-style spare rib preparation is a recognised competition barbecue cut, distinguished from baby back ribs by the removal of the rib tips and sternum. Low-and-slow oven technique adapted from American barbecue practice.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool the cooked rack, wrap tightly in foil, and freeze. Reheat in foil at 160°C for 25 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook through the full low phase a day ahead. Finish uncovered at 180°C for 20 minutes to reheat and set the bark.

content.text: St Louis-style spare ribs are a full rack of pork ribs trimmed flat by removing the cartilage tips and the sternum, which gives you a uniform rectangle of meat that cooks evenly and presents beautifully. Rubbed with a spiced mix, then cooked at 135°C for three and a half hours and finished uncovered to darken the crust, they come out with meat that pulls cleanly from the bone without falling off entirely. The texture and flavour are the reward for the time investment.

The thin papery membrane on the bone side of the rack must come off before cooking, or it turns leathery and prevents the rub from penetrating the meat from below. Loosen it at one end with a blunt knife, grip it with a piece of kitchen paper for purchase, and pull it off in one piece.

items.prepNote: St Louis-style or spare ribs, membrane removed

content.text: Heat the oven to 135°C (fan 115°C / gas mark 1). Mix the rub: {{paprika-smoked}}, {{dark-brown-sugar}}, {{sea-salt-flakes}}, {{black-pepper}}, {{garlic-powder}}, {{onion-powder}}, {{cayenne-pepper}}, {{mustard-powder}}.

Pat the {{pork-ribs}} dry. Pull off the membrane from the bone side: loosen one corner with a cutlery knife, grip it with kitchen paper, and peel it away. Coat the rack all over with the rub, pressing it firmly into the meat on both sides.

Lay the rack meat side up on a foil-lined baking tray. Cover tightly with foil. Cook at 135°C for two and a half to three hours, until the meat has pulled back from the bone ends by at least 1 cm and feels tender when pressed through the foil.
If using {{cider-vinegar}}, remove the foil after 90 minutes, spritz lightly over the surface, and re-cover. This keeps the surface moist and gives a slight tang to the crust.

Remove the foil entirely. Increase the oven to 180°C (fan 160°C / gas mark 4). Cook uncovered for a further 30 to 45 minutes until the rub has set into a dark, firm crust on the surface. The rack should be mahogany-coloured, not black.
Rest for ten minutes before cutting between the bones to serve. The meat should hold together when lifted but pull away from the bone with a light tug.

items.symptom: The membrane won't come off in one piece
items.cause: Not enough grip, or starting at the wrong end.
items.fix: Start at the thicker end of the rack. Use a piece of dry kitchen paper rather than a cloth: the dry paper grips the slippery membrane much better.

items.symptom: The meat is still tough after three hours
items.cause: Oven temperature too low, or the rack is very thick.
items.fix: Check the oven with a thermometer: older ovens often run cool. Add another 30 minutes at 135°C, covered, and test again by pressing the meat.

items.symptom: The rub crust is pale, not dark
items.cause: Uncovered phase cut too short, or oven temperature not high enough for the finish.
items.fix: The uncovered phase needs a really higher heat than the braise. Check the oven is at 180°C and give it a full 45 minutes uncovered.

items.symptom: The meat falls completely off the bone
items.fix: Still edible and tasty, just harder to serve neatly. Next time reduce the low phase by 30 minutes and test the texture earlier.

content.text: St Louis is a trimming style, not a cooking tradition. The Midwest meat-packing industry standardised the cut for uniform retail presentation. In competition barbecue, St Louis racks are the default format because the flat shape cooks evenly. At home, serve as a main with coleslaw, potato salad, and pickles.
